summary: Defined ways to cut the gap in connectivity when a Mobile IPv6 device moves between access routers. During handover, link switching and the standard protocol steps leave a period when the device cannot send or receive. The document set up procedures to anticipate and shorten that delay. It was replaced by RFC 5568.

plainLanguage.summary: When you switch between two Wi-Fi hotspots, your video call freezes for a moment. This was a plan for getting ready for the move beforehand, so the call hardly stops. It has since been replaced by RFC 5568.

subtitle: Protocol to reduce the delay when a mobile device switches between access routers.

tldr.problem: When a Mobile IPv6 device moves between access routers, there is a period of disconnection during link switching and IP protocol operations, causing noticeable delay for real-time applications like VoIP.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol allows the mobile device to anticipate the move by learning about neighboring routers beforehand, pre-configuring a new address, and establishing forwarding tunnels before physically switching links, operating in predictive or reactive modes.
tldr.outcome: Handover latency is significantly reduced, making real-time services more reliable during mobility. The protocol was updated with RFC 5568 in 2009.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: RtSolPr, PrRtAdv, FBU, FBack, HI, HAck, UNA

facts.label: Target delay reduction
facts.value: From 100s of milliseconds to 10s of milliseconds

today: RFC 5268 is a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 5568 in July 2009, which provides updates and refinements. Modern Mobile IPv6 Fast Handover implementations use RFC 5568.

sections.title: The Handover Problem
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 allows a mobile device to move between networks while maintaining its address and ongoing connections. However, when a device moves from one access router to another, several operations must happen: the link must switch, the device must detect the new subnet, it must configure a new address on the new subnet, and it must notify its home agent and communicating peers of its new location. These steps introduce handover latency.

For many applications, this latency is acceptable. However, real-time applications such as Voice over IP (VoIP) and video conferencing are sensitive to interruptions. Even a brief gap in connectivity can cause noticeable audio dropout or video stutter. Additionally, throughput-sensitive applications benefit from minimizing the gap. This RFC specifies a protocol to reduce handover latency by allowing preparation to occur before the physical movement happens.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving between networks normally means your phone loses connection for a moment while it figures out the new network. That moment breaks video calls. This RFC describes how to prepare for the move ahead of time so the break is shorter or invisible.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The protocol works by dividing the handover process into predictable steps that can be anticipated. The mobile node (MN) can use link-layer mechanisms to discover nearby access points, then send a Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr) to its current access router (Previous Access Router, or PAR). The PAR responds with a Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) message containing information about neighboring access routers, including their IP addresses, link-layer addresses, and subnet prefixes.

With this information, the mobile node can formulate a prospective new Care-of Address (NCoA) for the new access router (NAR) while still connected to the PAR. It then sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to the PAR, which establishes a binding between the mobile node's current address and the new address. The PAR begins tunneling packets meant for the old address to the new address.

When the mobile node physically moves to the new access router, it immediately announces its presence with an Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement (UNA) message. The new router can now forward both arriving packets and buffered packets to the mobile node. The entire process reduces the disruption window from several hundred milliseconds to just a few tens of milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: Before moving, the phone asks its current router about nearby routers. It gets their addresses and picks a new address for itself ahead of time. It tells the old router to start forwarding its packets to the new location. When it switches, it just says 'hello' to the new router and immediately gets its packets.

sections.title: Predictive and Reactive Modes
sections.content:
The protocol operates in two modes. In predictive mode, the mobile node sends the FBU while still attached to the PAR and receives a Fast Binding Acknowledgment (FBack) before moving. By the time it switches to the NAR, packet forwarding is already active, minimizing any gap. This mode is ideal when the device has advance warning of the handover, such as from link-layer triggers indicating weakening signal strength from the current access point and stronger signal from a nearby one.

In reactive mode, the mobile node cannot send the FBU before moving. This might happen if the handover occurs unexpectedly or if the device did not receive an FBack before losing connection. In this case, the mobile node sends the FBU from the new access router's link, after sending the UNA. While less optimal, this still reduces latency compared to standard Mobile IPv6 because address pre-configuration eliminates the delay of address auto-configuration.

The protocol also supports network-initiated handover, where the network itself sends an unsolicited PrRtAdv to advise the mobile node that a handover is imminent. Some wireless technologies use this approach for network-controlled mobility.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to do it: the phone can prepare while still on the old network (the good way), or it can start preparing after it switches (the backup way). Either way, the result is less delay than without the protocol.

sections.title: Message Types and Handover Signaling
sections.content:
The protocol introduces several new ICMPv6 messages. The Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr), sent by the MN, contains link-layer addresses of access points and requests information about them. The Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) contains tuples of (Access Point Identifier, Router Information), allowing the MN to map nearby access points to their corresponding routers and prefixes.

The Fast Binding Update (FBU) message is sent to the PAR to establish the forwarding tunnel. It must include a Binding Authorization Data for FMIPv6 (BADF) option to prevent unauthorized parties from establishing bindings. The Fast Binding Acknowledgment (FBack) confirms that the tunnel is established and the NCoA is acceptable.

Between routers, the PAR and NAR exchange Handover Initiate (HI) and Handover Acknowledge (HAck) messages to coordinate the handover. The HI message informs the NAR about an incoming mobile node and allows it to prepare forwarding and buffering. The NAR responds with HAck, confirming readiness or, in assigned addressing mode, providing an alternative address for the MN to use.

Upon arrival at the new network, the mobile node sends an Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement (UNA) message to indicate its presence and cause the NAR to transition from proactive to reactive packet forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol uses several types of messages: the phone asks about neighbors, the old router describes them, the phone tells the old router where it is going, routers coordinate, and finally the phone says hello to the new router.

sections.title: Key Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol addresses several important practical considerations. Packet buffering at the new router can prevent loss of packets arriving before the mobile node sends UNA. The RFC specifies a default algorithm for releasing buffered packets that attempts to respect the original arrival rate.

The protocol supports both stateless address auto-configuration (where the MN picks its own address from the prefix) and assigned addressing (where the router picks an address for the MN). In assigned addressing mode, the HAck message can provide an alternative address, allowing routers to handle policy-based address allocation.

Duplicate Address Detection (DAD), normally required before using a new address, is performed by the NAR before defending the prospective address, reducing delay. However, in deployments where address collisions are extremely unlikely, DAD can be disabled.

The RFC also addresses fast and erroneous movement, where a mobile node moves faster than the signaling can handle or moves to an unexpected location. Short-lived tunnels (on the order of a few tens of seconds) and explicit tunnel termination via FBU with lifetime zero help manage these edge cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol handles several real-world issues: what if packets arrive while the phone is switching, what if the router assigns addresses instead of the phone picking them, and what if the phone moves unexpectedly.

sections.title: Evolution and Current Status
sections.content: RFC 5268 obsoletes RFC 4068, the previous Fast Handovers specification from 2005. The updates include clarifications, improved message handling, and deprecation of the Fast Neighbor Advertisement (FNA) message in favor of the standard Unsolicited Neighbor Advertisement. The protocol was further updated by RFC 5568 in 2009, which incorporated additional improvements and refined the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC updated an earlier version of the same protocol. An even newer version (RFC 5568) came out in 2009 with more improvements. Modern implementations use RFC 5568.
